title: Housing approvals: San Francisco against eight other cities
question: By the cities' own reports to the State, how long does housing take to move from application to entitlement, to building permit, to completion, and how much gets built?
finding: Across report years 2018 to 2025, San Francisco's median was 377 days from application to entitlement (rank 2 of 9, 1 being slowest), 254 days from entitlement to building permit (rank 3 of 9) and 561 days from permit to completion (rank 2 of 9). The slowest city on each measure was San Jose (433 days), San Jose (579) and Oakland (591). Oakland, Fresno reported the same date for application and entitlement on most projects, a difference in reporting rather than in speed. San Francisco reported 29,819 homes completed, 4.43 per 1,000 residents a year (rank 3 of 8 with a population figure, 1 being most).
how: Rows are the projects each city reported to the State. Application to entitlement joins Table A to Table A2 on the city's own tracking number; entitlement to permit joins rows on the parcel number, taking the first permit on or after the entitlement; permit to completion joins on the tracking number. Medians cover intervals of 0 to 3,650 days ending in a report year, with at least 10 linked projects. Homes per 1,000 residents divide the units each city reported by its population, summed over the years with a population figure.
limits: Each city fills in the dates by its own definitions, and the mix differs: most Los Angeles rows are accessory units and San Diego reports almost no entitlement dates. San Francisco files entitlements under a Planning record and permits under a building permit number, so only its parcel number links the two and few projects link. A parcel with two projects can be mis-joined. Projects that never reach the next stage are not counted, which flatters slow cities. The State department's 2023 review quoted averages on 2022 data, which are higher than these medians. Population comes from the Census for San Francisco and from the State Controller for the others; none is on disk for Berkeley. Unit counts are as each city reported them and a project can appear in more than one report year; the City's own count of net homes completed, used in the permit records screens, is lower.
